theming.text: Colours, track and height are CSS custom properties: --pass-color-very-weak to --pass-color-strong, --pass-track and --pass-height. Play with them here; the CSS below follows along.

binding.note: Every meter on this page speaks your language. The playground gives each one the texts of the language you pick at the top, and its accessible name. To keep the snippets short, only the translation demos show how; the show and hide button in the fields belongs to the playground, not to the package.

home.title: Password strength, measured honestly.
home.lead: Passcore estimates how hard a password is to guess, checks it against your rules and tells people what to fix, in their own language. A tiny core with no dependencies, plus ready-made meters for jQuery, plain JavaScript, React, Vue and Svelte.

features.title: Honest numbers, clear words, any framework

estimate.title: Estimates, not wishful thinking
estimate.text: Length comes first. Repeats, sequences, keyboard runs and common passwords are worth almost nothing, even in leetspeak: P@ssw0rd! is not a strong password.

rules.title: Rules people understand
rules.text: Minimum length, character classes, common passwords and personal details. The first rule that fails becomes the message, so people know what to fix next.

a11y.title: Accessible markup
a11y.text: A real role="meter" with a spoken value, a polite live region for the message, and aria-describedby tying the field to it.

i18n.title: In any language
i18n.text: Texts in i18next’s JSON format, plural forms included. English, Spanish and Catalan ship with every binding, or bring your own t.

theme.title: Themed with seven properties
theme.text: Colours, track and height are CSS custom properties: match your design system without fighting specificity.

core.title: A core with no dependencies
core.text: @passcore/core touches no DOM and holds no texts: it returns data and message keys, so it runs anywhere, servers included.

bindings.title: Pick your stack
bindings.lead: Every binding renders the same markup with the same stylesheet, so moving between frameworks doesn’t change what people see.

jquery.title: jQuery plugin
jquery.lead: @passcore/jquery adds $.fn.password() to jQuery 3 and 4. Point it at a password input and it appends an accessible meter to the closest container, and fires events as people type.

demo.checklist: The classic signup form: every condition, red or green as people type. password.score brings the full result, and result.rules lists every enabled rule, in order, with its id, passed and params. The plugin reads the username when the password changes, so its field triggers an update too. Every item stays grey until something is typed: an empty password is “not common” too, and saying so in green would mislead.
demo.default: Out of the box, the meter waits out of sight until the field gets focus, then slides in. It slides away again if the field is left empty.
demo.always: With animate: false the meter is there from the start, and showPercent adds the number.
demo.linked: With userInputs the password can’t contain the username: try typing it in both fields. The fields are read on every keystroke.
demo.translations: The bundled files go in translations, and locale picks the plural forms. Switch the language at the top: the plugin reads its texts once, so the playground mounts it again.
demo.i18next: translate takes the t of an i18next instance, here the playground’s own. The plugin only rewrites the message when it changes, so a language change needs a fresh mount.
demo.events: password.score fires on every keystroke with the percent and the full result. Here it drives the score and the Send button.
demo.group: The meter goes to the closest div by default. With closestSelector: '.form-group' it lands below the whole input group instead.

vanilla.title: Vanilla JavaScript
vanilla.lead: @passcore/vanilla needs no framework and no jQuery: call createPasswordMeter() on an input, or write a <passcore-meter> element where you want the meter.

demo.checklist: The classic signup form: every condition, red or green as people type. The onScore callback (or the bubbling passcore:score event) brings the full result, and result.rules lists every enabled rule, in order, with its id, passed and params. Typing a username calls refresh(), so the personal details rule follows it. Every item stays grey until something is typed: an empty password is “not common” too, and saying so in green would mislead.
demo.default: With hideUntilFocus the meter stays hidden until the field gets focus, and hides again on blur while the field is empty.
demo.always: Without hideUntilFocus the meter is shown from the start, and showPercent adds the number.
demo.linked: With userInputs the password can’t contain the username. Strings are selectors, read on every keystroke; functions work too.
demo.translations: The bundled files go in translations, locale picks the plural forms and label names the meter for screen readers. The options are read once, so a new language means a new meter.
demo.i18next: translate takes the t of an i18next instance, here the playground’s own. Texts are translated on every update, so refresh() is all a language change needs.
demo.events: The onScore callback and the bubbling passcore:score event both get the percent on every update. Here they drive the Send button and the score.
demo.group: The meter goes right after the input by default. container appends it elsewhere: here, below the whole input group.
demo.element: <passcore-meter> renders the meter where you write it. Attributes cover the simple options: min-length, show-percent, user-inputs, locale, label and a few more.
demo.options: What attributes can’t hold (translations, rules, callbacks) goes in the options property, merged over the attributes. This one also asks for a number and a symbol.

react.title: React
react.lead: @passcore/react brings a controlled <PasswordStrengthMeter> component and the usePasswordStrength() hook, for React 18 and later.

demo.checklist: The classic signup form, built with your own markup: usePasswordStrength() returns the result, and result.rules lists every enabled rule, in order, with its id, passed and params. The component draws the bar next to it. Every item stays grey until something is typed: an empty password is “not common” too, and saying so in green would mislead.
demo.default: The component is controlled: it takes the password as a prop and never touches your input. It has no hidden state, so the meter is always shown; id links it to the field.
demo.percent: showPercent adds the number next to the bar.
demo.linked: With userInputs the password can’t contain the username. Pass the current values, straight from state.
demo.translations: The bundled files go in translations, locale picks the plural forms and label names the meter for screen readers. Switch the language at the top: new props, new texts.
demo.i18next: translate takes the t of an i18next instance, here the playground’s own. The function never changes, so locale tells the component when to translate again.
demo.events: onScore gets the percent whenever the result changes (never on mount). Here it drives the score and the Send button.
demo.group: The meter is just another element: put it after the input group and it spans the whole group.

vue.title: Vue
vue.lead: @passcore/vue brings a <PasswordStrengthMeter> component and the usePasswordStrength() composable, for Vue 3.5 and later.

demo.checklist: The classic signup form, built with your own markup: the usePasswordStrength() composable returns the result as a ref, and result.rules lists every enabled rule, in order, with its id, passed and params. The component draws the bar next to it. Every item stays grey until something is typed: an empty password is “not common” too, and saying so in green would mislead.
demo.default: The component gets the password as a prop, so it works with any v-model. It is always shown; id links it to the field.
demo.percent: show-percent adds the number next to the bar.
demo.linked: With user-inputs the password can’t contain the username. Pass the current values, straight from your refs.
demo.translations: The bundled files go in translations, locale picks the plural forms and label names the meter for screen readers. Switch the language at the top: new props, new texts.
demo.i18next: translate takes the t of an i18next instance, here the playground’s own. The function never changes, so locale tells the component when to translate again.
demo.events: The score event brings the percent whenever the result changes (never on mount). Here it drives the score and the Send button.
demo.group: The meter is just another element: put it after the input group and it spans the whole group.

svelte.title: Svelte
svelte.lead: @passcore/svelte brings a <PasswordStrengthMeter> component and passwordStrength(), a rune-based helper, for Svelte 5.

demo.checklist: The classic signup form, built with your own markup: passwordStrength() returns the result as a getter, and result.rules lists every enabled rule, in order, with its id, passed and params. The component draws the bar next to it. Every item stays grey until something is typed: an empty password is “not common” too, and saying so in green would mislead.
demo.default: The component gets the password as a prop, so bind:value on your input is all it takes. It is always shown; id links it to the field.
demo.percent: showPercent adds the number next to the bar.
demo.linked: With userInputs the password can’t contain the username. Pass the current values, straight from your state.
demo.translations: The bundled files go in translations, locale picks the plural forms and label names the meter for screen readers. Switch the language at the top: new props, new texts.
demo.i18next: translate takes the t of an i18next instance, here the playground’s own. The function never changes, so locale tells the component when to translate again.
demo.events: onscore gets the percent whenever the result changes (never on mount). Here it drives the score and the Send button.
demo.group: The meter is just another element: put it after the input group and it spans the whole group.
